howItWorks.title: How scoring works
howItWorks.subtitle: Every score breaks down into three independent checks, weighted and shown in full. Nothing is hidden, and nothing is inferred by a language model — every point traces back to a rule you can read for yourself.
howItWorks.weightedAverageIntro: The overall score is this weighted average — nothing more. That formula lives as plain code (
howItWorks.weightedAverageOutro: in the backend), not a black-box model call.
howItWorks.traceSubtitle: Not an example of how it works. The actual mechanism, step by step.
howItWorks.noAiBody: Nothing above is generated, summarized, or judged by a language model. The score and every finding behind it come from deterministic rules — the same input always produces the same output, and every rule is visible in the source. Your resume is parsed, scored, and discarded; nothing is stored.

keywordOverlap.name: Keyword overlap
keywordOverlap.summary: The most direct signal of fit: does the resume actually contain what this specific job description asks for.
keywordOverlap.detail: Both the resume and the job description are run through the same rule-based keyword extractor — a curated taxonomy of skills and tools, matched by exact text and fuzzy variants (so "JavaScript" and "JS" count as the same skill, but "Java" never silently matches inside "JavaScript"). Every skill the job description asks for is checked against the resume, and every match or gap is listed by name.
keywordOverlap.example1: "Python" — matched, found in the Skills section
keywordOverlap.example2: "Docker" — matched, found in the Experience section

completeness.name: Completeness
completeness.summary: A secondary quality signal, independent of any specific job: is the resume itself well-formed.
completeness.detail: A fixed set of structural checks — no interpretation, no scoring on writing quality or tone. Each either passes or fails.
completeness.example1: "contact_has_email" — a real email address was found in the contact section
completeness.example2: "experience_has_dates" — at least one work entry has a date range
completeness.example3: "bullets_quantified" — at least half of experience bullets contain a number

formatting.name: Formatting red flags
formatting.summary: A secondary risk signal for real-world ATS parsing, independent of any specific job.
formatting.detail: Checks for layout choices that are known to break real applicant tracking systems — not because they look bad, but because many ATS parsers read left-to-right, top-to-bottom and can silently scramble or drop content that doesn't follow that shape.
formatting.example1: "single_column_layout" — no multi-column or table-based layout detected
formatting.example2: "standard_section_headers" — every section header matches a recognized name
formatting.example3: "no_embedded_images" — no text is hidden inside an image the parser can't read

step1.label: Job description says
step1.content: "...3+ years of experience with AWS or similar cloud infrastructure..."

step2.label: Extractor scans for known terms
step2.content: The taxonomy has "AWS" as a canonical skill with the alias "Amazon Web Services". The word "AWS" appears in the text with a clean word boundary — not buried inside another word.

step3.label: Exact match found
step3.content: Rule: word-boundary match on "AWS" → canonical skill AWS, added to the job description's required-skill list.

step4.label: Resume is checked for the same skill
step4.content: Your resume's Skills section is scanned with the identical extractor. If "AWS" or any of its aliases appears anywhere in Skills, Experience, or Summary, it's recorded as matched — along with which section it came from.

step5.label: Result
step5.content: "AWS" — matched, found in the Experience section. This exact line is what appears in your results.
